sweep_summary: Siwi (siwi1239) is in the catalog as set by morphology on Schiattarella 2015 (EPHE thesis, ch. 9). this search of works with stress in the title listed three items: Schiattarella 2020 (Language Science Press chapter, Glottolog 643847) and two Glottolog records (50696, 99033) that are one and the same JEP 2004 paper by Louali & Philippson. All were obtained open and read. chapter and whole volume saved) is a first-hand, peer-reviewed English statement of the noun-accent rule (isolated noun final except kinship; preposition/possessive = penult; discourse final = indefinite/first mention vs penult = definite/anaphoric, with demonstratives, detached constructions, relatives and locatives overriding) — it CONFIRMS and REFINES the catalog's classification but does not cover verbs first-hand and does not supersede the thesis, whose ch. 9 is the fuller statement (the chapter is essentially the published English version of thesis §9.2). Louali & Philippson 2004 (open on afcp-parole.org, held by the project since 09-16) is the original first-hand source for the verb-initial vs noun-final split the catalog quotes second-hand, with the VC-preterite exception and the schwa-accentable claim; it CONFIRMS. Also read (held by the project from 09-16, not in the item list): Kaland & Schiattarella 2025 (TAI, open), the first acoustic corpus study, which finds right-edge prominence (final in disyllables, penult in trisyllables) and leaves the definiteness shift unconfirmed — a refinement, not a contradiction. Not obtainable: Louali & Philippson 2005 Faits de Langues 26 (Brill paywall/CAPTCHA; HIGH priority — the fullest rule statement per every source read), and the Köppe print volumes Louali 2003, Vycichl 2005, Naumann 2012, Souag 2013 (medium). No item contradicts the catalog. downloads were done by direct URL (Zenodo API, langsci-press catalog, Crossref API).

new_statements.quote: Accent on nouns in Siwi is insensitive to quantity as it can fall on the last or penultimate syllable of the same noun. Several authors agree that the accent on the last syllable codes indefiniteness and the accent on the penultimate syllable codes definiteness. [p.152] ... Nouns, when isolated, carry the accent on the last syllable and, when preceded by a preposition, they carry it on the penultimate syllable. ... My data confirm those presented by Louali & Philippson (2005), who state that the accent on the noun (except for kinship terms) falls on the last syllable: (1) aggʷíd aggʷidán (2) taltí təltawén. However ... if the noun is preceded by a preposition, the accent is on the penultimate syllable: (3) agbə́n g ágbən (4) amán i áman (5) ulí sg úli [p.155]
new_statements.citation: Schiattarella, Valentina. 2020. Accent on nouns and its reference coding in Siwi Berber (Egypt). In K. Balogh, A. Latrouite & R. D. Van Valin Jr. (eds.), Nominal anchoring, 149-170. Berlin: Language Science Press. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.4049687
new_statements.reading: Peer-reviewed, English, first-hand corpus statement (fieldwork 2011-2018, PRAAT-verified) of the Siwi noun-accent rule: quantity-insensitive, citation-form final (kinship terms penult), penult after a preposition or possessive, and a discourse alternation final (indefinite / first mention / presentational) vs penult (definite / anaphoric / identifiable / unique), which the author herself says is 'too simplistic' as a bare definiteness rule because demonstratives, detached constructions, relatives and locatives override it. Verb accent (first stem syllable) is cited from Louali & Philippson 2004, not restated first-hand. This supports the catalog's set by morphology coding: placement is set by word class, morphosyntax and reference status within a right-edge two-syllable window, not by weight or a fixed position.

sources.note: First-hand corpus study (fieldwork 2011-2018, PRAAT-checked; higher pitch is the only consistent cue, p.153). Noun accent is quantity-insensitive and alternates between final and penult on the same noun: isolated noun = final (kinship terms excepted); preposition + noun = penult (in elicitation; in discourse an indefinite noun keeps final accent even after a preposition, p.157); possessive clitic = always penult (p.161); proper nouns, toponyms, kinship terms = penult (p.160); locative on toponyms = final (p.164); in discourse final = first mention / presentational / non-anaphoric, penult = an…

Proc. 3rd International Conference on Tone and Intonation (TAI 2025), Herrsching, 50-54. doi:10.21437/TAI.2025-11 [not in the works with stress in the title list; downloaded in the 09-16 pass]

sources.quote: Literature review restates the morphosyntactic system (nouns final, kinship penult, prepositions retract 1 or 2 syllables, possessives penult, verbs stem-initial, ga-/la-/perfect rules) and notes Naumann 2012 'did not treat stress extensively' and that 'an overall description of stress placement … across all word classes, is lacking'. First bottom-up acoustic study (7 speakers, spontaneous narratives; adverbs, nouns, prepositions only): 'The most prominent syllable in disyllables is the ultimate, whereas the most prominent syllable in trisyllables is the penultimate'; prominence 'tends to be f
sources.note: First acoustic corpus study (899 syllables, 7 speakers, spontaneous narratives; verbs excluded). Prominence sits at the right edge (final in disyllables, penult in trisyllables); the definiteness shift was neither confirmed nor rejected. Its §1 also states that 'an overall description of stress placement, i.e., an outline of its phonological rules across all word classes, is lacking' (p.51). Refines rather than overturns the catalog: right-edge two-syllable window holds; whether word length or morphology drives the shift is left open.

sources.quote: 'pour le nom, l'accent tombe sur la dernière syllabe du mot dans la forme de citation … pour le verbe, l'accent porte sur la première syllabe du thème' with one phonological constraint ('au prétérit, une syllabe initiale de thème du type V(C) ne peut être accentuée et l’accent se reporte sur la syllabe suivante'); preposition+noun retracts accent one syllable (talti vs i-talti); resultative -a puts accent on the penult. Discussion: 'L'attribution de l'accent ne se pose pas en termes de contraintes phonologiques liées à la structure et/ou à la nature de la syllabe, sauf pour le prétérit des ver
sources.note: Translation: for the noun, accent falls on the last syllable of the word in citation form; for the verb, accent falls on the first syllable of the stem. Although accent is assigned morphologically (first stem syllable), there is one phonological constraint: in the preterite a stem-initial V(C) syllable cannot be accented and accent moves to the next syllable, even a suffix. [Discussion] Accent assignment is not a matter of phonological constraints tied to syllable structure or type, except for the preterite of vowel-initial verbs; all vowels including schwa are accentable. sources.quote: (not read) As reported by Kaland & Schiattarella 2025 p.50: 'nouns in isolation have ultimate stress, kinship terms have penultimate stress. As for the role of prepositions, they specify how some (i, s, n, af, d) have the consequence of moving the accent one syllable back, while others (g, sg) two [5]. With possessive clitics, stress is always on the penultimate syllable ... Adjectives have stress on the last syllable, as nouns, when in isolation, and on the penultimate when preceded by n ... Adverbs in general have stress on the penultimate syllable.'
